records.text: Visual BERT models captions and images jointly.
Visual BERT uses a fixed pretrained object detection system such as Faster R-CNN to cut out objects.
Visual BERT embeds the cut-out objects into vectors via CNNs and special positional embeddings.
Visual BERT feeds the object vectors along with the caption into a single Transformer.
Visual BERT is pretrained using masked language modeling.
Visual BERT is pretrained using sentence-image prediction.
Sentence-image prediction distinguishes whether a given caption matches the image.
Sample attention heads in Visual BERT show how words from the caption attend to corresponding objects.
Vision Transformer (ViT; Dosovitsky et al., 2020) is the most successful Transformer-based architecture for images.
ViT is a straightforward modification of BERT.
ViT uses only image-based tokens as input (no text).
In ViT, the input image is cut into small patches.
The original image in ViT has dimensions $H \times W$ and $C$ channels.
The image is transformed into a sequence of patches of size $P \times P$ in ViT.
The number of patches $N$ in ViT is $HW/P^2$.
The patch sequence tensor in ViT has shape $N \times P^2 \times C$.
In ViT, patches are turned into embeddings via a simple linear projection.
The sequence of patch embeddings in ViT is fed into a Transformer encoder.
The Transformer encoder in ViT is identical to BERT's encoder.
ViT is pretrained using masked patch modeling.
Masked patch modeling replaces half of the input embeddings with a learnable `[mask]` embedding.
Masked patch modeling is analogous to masked language modeling.
ViT uses positional encodings.
ViT uses the same absolute positional encoding as the original Transformer.
Experiments using 2D positional encodings in ViT showed no difference in results.
Swin Transformer (Liu et al., 2021) is similar to ViT.
Swin Transformer is built in a hierarchical fashion.
Swin Transformer processes image patches on several scales.
Swin Transformer computes self-attention across patches in a convolutional-like architecture.
In Swin Transformer, windows shift between self-attention layers.
The shifting windows provide connections between different parts of the image.
The Swin Transformer architecture progressively reduces the spatial geometry.
The progressive reduction of spatial geometry in Swin Transformer is analogous to classical CNN backbones.
Swin Transformer can scale up to larger input resolutions.
Swin Transformer is suitable for dense recognition tasks such as image segmentation.
Swin Transformer v2 is a later iteration of Swin Transformer.
Swin Transformer v2 scaled up to 3 billion parameters.
Swin Transformer v2 allowed training with images up to $1536 \times 1536$ pixels.
Swin Transformer v2 improved state of the art across image processing tasks.
DeepMind's Perceiver (Jaegle et al., 2021a) is a general-purpose architecture.
Perceiver can process numerous modalities without modality-specific encoders.
The main idea of Perceiver is to avoid the quadratic bottleneck of self-attention.
Perceiver uses lower-dimensional latent units as queries.
In Perceiver, a small vector of latents attends to large byte arrays for keys and values.
Perceiver can be trained on images, point clouds, audio, and video with no change to the architecture.
Perceiver's attention maps can go down to individual pixels.
Perceiver IO extends Perceiver to handle high-dimensional outputs.
Perceiver IO handles multi-task language understanding.
Perceiver IO handles dense visual tasks such as optical flow.
Perceiver IO handles hybrid dense/sparse multimodal tasks, such as video+audio+class autoencoding.
Perceiver IO handles tasks with symbolic outputs, such as StarCraft II.
In Perceiver IO, output queries are constructed automatically by combining vectors describing properties of the current output (e.g., position coordinates).
Basic classification architectures are insufficient for computer vision tasks.
Object detection is the problem of determining the locations of objects using CNNs.
R-CNN looks for bounding boxes using an external algorithm, such as selective search.
R-CNN extracts CNN features for each proposed bounding box.
The CNN in R-CNN is pretrained on ImageNet and fine-tuned on the target dataset.
R-CNN classifies each proposed region.
Visualisations of R-CNN show regions of activation for a neuron from a high layer.
R-CNN additionally uses bounding box regression to localise objects.
The bounding box regression in R-CNN uses a linear regression on features from the last pooling layer.
R-CNN was excellent for its time.
R-CNN won the ILSVRC 2013 detection challenge.
The ILSVRC 2013 detection challenge had 200 classes.
R-CNN required multiple training stages: training a CNN, then an SVM on CNN features, then bounding box regressors.
R-CNN training was very long because features had to be extracted for every region proposal and written to disk.
R-CNN recognition was slow, taking about 47 seconds per image even on a GPU.
The slowness of R-CNN was because a full CNN forward pass was needed for each proposal.
Fast R-CNN addresses the problems of R-CNN.
Fast R-CNN uses RoI (Region of Interest) projection.
In Fast R-CNN, only one pass of the main CNN is done over the whole image.
Fast R-CNN then crops and pools features for each region.
The loss function in Fast R-CNN is the sum of classification error and bounding box regression error.
Fast R-CNN is two orders of magnitude faster than R-CNN with no loss of quality.
Fast R-CNN still uses selective search for region proposals.
Adding more region proposal candidates in Fast R-CNN did not help much.
In R-CNN and Fast R-CNN, selective search for generating proposals was a bottleneck.
Faster R-CNN embeds proposal generation inside the network.
Faster R-CNN adds a separate Region Proposal Network (RPN).
The RPN evaluates each possibility from a set of predefined anchor boxes.
Faster R-CNN was a very strong detector.
Faster R-CNN was the best across all evaluation metrics on Pascal VOC 2007 and 2012 at the time.
Faster R-CNN is still relevant today.
YOLO detects both bounding boxes and object classes in a single pass.
In YOLO, the image is split into an $S \times S$ grid.
In YOLO, each grid cell predicts bounding boxes and class probabilities.
In the original YOLO, the predictions are combined as $p(\text{class}_i \mid \text{obj}) \cdot p(\text{obj}) \cdot \text{IOU}_{\text{bbox}}$.
In later refinements of YOLO, the combined score simplifies to $p(\text{class}_i) \cdot \text{IOU}$.
The output tensor in YOLO has size $S \times S \times (5B + C)$.
Each bounding box prediction in YOLO consists of $(x, y, w, h)$ and a confidence score.
YOLO is trained end-to-end with a single loss function.
The YOLO loss function uses an indicator $\mathbb{1}_{\text{obj}}^{ij}$ which is 1 if the $j$-th bounding box predictor in cell $i$ is responsible for an object that is present.
YOLO has slightly lower accuracy than Faster R-CNN.
YOLO is much faster than Faster R-CNN.
YOLO works out-of-the-box.
Classical object detectors (R-CNN, Faster R-CNN, YOLO, SSD) rely on hand-designed components.
The hand-designed components include a dense grid of anchor boxes, region proposals, and non-maximum suppression (NMS) to remove duplicate predictions.
In classical detectors, anchors and NMS are not learned end-to-end.
Anchors and NMS require careful manual tuning.
NMS is a non-differentiable post-processing step bolted on after the network.
Treating object detection as a direct set prediction problem means using a Transformer to predict the whole set of objects at once, with no anchors and no NMS.
DETR is based on the idea of set prediction.
DETR opened the door to Transformer-based detectors that currently dominate the field.
DETR is a direct adaptation of Transformers for object detection.
DETR treats object detection as a set prediction task.
DETR uses a set-based global loss.
The set-based global loss enforces unique predictions through bipartite matching.
DETR uses an encoder-decoder Transformer architecture.
DETR uses a conventional convolutional backbone, such as ResNet.
DETR flattens the features from the backbone.
DETR adds positional encoding to the flattened features.
The flattened and encoded features are processed by a Transformer encoder.
In DETR, the decoder receives a small fixed number of learnable object queries.
The object queries are positional embeddings that attend to the encoder output.
In DETR, a small feedforward network on top of the decoder outputs class labels and bounding boxes.
The class labels include a “no object” class.
DETR's loss function uses a set of predictions $\hat{y}$ of size $N$ and ground-truth objects $y$ padded with $\varnothing$ to size $N$.
The optimal permutation $\sigma^*$ in DETR's loss is found by minimizing the sum of matching costs via the Hungarian algorithm.
The matching cost is $-\mathbf{1}[c_i \neq \varnothing] \hat{p}_{\sigma(i)}(c_i) + \mathbf{1}[c_i \neq \varnothing] \ell_{\text{box}}(b_i, \hat{b}_{\sigma(i)})$.
In the matching cost, $\ell_{\text{box}}$ combines IoU and $L_1$ losses.
The training loss in DETR is $\sum_{i=1}^N \left( -\log \hat{p}_{\sigma^*(i)}(c_i) + \mathbf{1}[c_i \neq \varnothing] \ell_{\text{box}}(b_i, \hat{b}_{\sigma(i)}) \right)$.
In practice, the “no object” predictions are down-weighted in the loss.
DETR provides good detection results.
DETR distributes object instances across attention heads.
In DETR, decoder attention for each object is localised to object boundaries.
DETR likely separates object instances via global attention in the encoder.
The decoder in DETR handles class and boundary refinement.
DETR struggles with small objects.
DETR's quadratic complexity makes multi-scale detection difficult.
Deformable DETR replaces standard self-attention with deformable attention.
Deformable attention attends only to a few sampling points around a reference location.
Deformable attention dramatically reduces complexity.
Deformable attention enables multi-scale feature processing.
DAB-DETR reintroduces the idea of anchor boxes.
In DAB-DETR, the anchor boxes are learnable.
The anchor boxes in DAB-DETR are gradually refined from layer to layer in the decoder.
In DAB-DETR, the anchor box width and height modulate cross-attention.
This modulation leads to better localised attention.
This modulation leads to faster training.
SMCA DETR modulates attention weights through spatial priors.
In SMCA DETR, nearby locations are given higher importance based on predicted offsets relative to reference points.
Optimal bipartite matching in DETR is unstable early in training.
Small weight changes can cause completely different assignments.
DN-DETR adds a training objective to reconstruct noisy ground truth boxes.
The noisy ground truth boxes in DN-DETR are fed via additional denoising queries.
The denoising objective in DN-DETR improves offset prediction.
Denoising queries serve as “good anchors” for learning offsets, keeping anchors closer to their targets.
DINO adds negative examples: anchors with large noise that have no nearby ground-truth objects.
These negative examples force the model to reject them.
DINO uses mixed query selection: positional queries are initialised from encoder proposals.
In DINO, content queries remain learnable and independent.
DINO introduces two-step lookahead.
In two-step lookahead, bounding box quality depends on the current anchor and the current offset prediction.
Deformable DETR blocked gradient backpropagation to stabilise training.
DINO blocks gradients one step further, updating layer $i$ parameters based on auxiliary losses from boxes $b_i$ and $b_{i+1}$.
DINO achieves very good results with fast training using a ResNet-50 backbone.
In H-Deformable-DETR, during training, the few positive examples are copied by adding additional queries that predict the same ground truth boxes.
Attention masks separate query groups in H-Deformable-DETR.
UP-DETR adds unsupervised pretraining.
In UP-DETR's pretraining, a random patch is taken and DETR must predict its position and reconstruct its features.
This pretraining preserves semantics without needing classification labels.
DETReg uses objects or regions found by external algorithms (e.g., selective search) instead of random crops during self-supervised pretraining.
DETReg predicts embeddings for these pseudo-objects.
Co-DETR attaches several auxiliary heads from other object detection models.
These auxiliary heads introduce new positive examples through matching to improve training.
A survey by Shehzadi et al. (2023) provides an overview of the DETR family of methods.
Object detection is one of the most interesting and hardest problems in computer vision.
Object detection's output structure is quite unusual compared to segmentation.
Usually, in vision tasks, the Transformer just replaces some part of the architecture and serves as a better feature extractor, without conceptually changing the architecture.
In segmentation, the UNet architecture from 2015 is still used; modern versions simply replace convolutional layers with self-attention layers.
The Transformer did not make UNet obsolete.
VisualBERT was one of the first more or less successful approaches to handling pictures with Transformers.
VisualBERT was mostly used for captioning.
To use VisualBERT, one would first solve object detection to obtain rectangles corresponding to objects in the image.
Then, one would pass the rectangles through a simple embedding layer to get a feature vector.
For the Transformer, it matters little whether the input came from text or images, as long as it is a sequence of vectors.
The Transformer is great at finding internal correlations and structure among these vectors.
The most striking feature of the Vision Transformer (ViT) is its simplicity.
There is absolutely no change in the Transformer architecture in ViT just because the input is an image.
In the original ViT paper, the authors show that they tried several ideas for positional encodings and none of them help.
ViT can simply treat the image patches as a sequence and use standard positional encodings from text Transformers.
ViT revolutionized computer vision and image processing.
Transformers extract better, more semantically rich features compared to convolutional networks.
In many applications, one can replace a convolutional network with ViT, reuse the same top layers, and achieve better performance.
Hundreds of papers did exactly this after 2020.
ViT and any Transformer have quadratic complexity.
The attention weights form a token-by-token matrix of size L×L, where L is the input length.
ViT’s complexity is quadratic in the number of patches.
If the image has height h, width w, and k×k patches, the number of patches is (h/k)(w/k), and the attention matrix scales as the square of that number.
ViT cannot go down to the level of individual pixels because a million pixels squared is too heavy.
ViT must use relatively big patches, which makes it hard to capture small details.
In object detection, if a small object like a cat is entirely inside one patch or on the boundary, details get lost when flattening patches into vectors.
There is no correct patch size: too big loses detail, too small is computationally infeasible.
The Swin Transformer is one of the most popular backbones today, alongside ViT.
Swin stands for shifted windows.
The Swin Transformer breaks down the image into parts and processes each part with patches.
Dividing into smaller windows significantly reduces computation because complexity is quadratic in the number of patches.
For example, a 2×2 grid of windows, each with a 3×3 patch grid, yields a local complexity of 9², 6², etc., summing to a few hundred, whereas a 25×25 patch grid would cost 25².
Quadratic complexity in Swin becomes effectively linear in the total size, quadratic only in the window size.

Swin uses a hierarchical structure: first cut the large image into small pieces (e.g., a 4×4 grid), process each part with a ViT, then combine them, process again, and finally process globally with ViT layers.
The SWIN transformer deals with 16 tokens at the input (4×4 grids).
In three steps, SWIN goes from a 16×16 image to a 4×4 image, which is then compressed into features or a single vector.
Shifted windows addresses the problem that when looking at small parts of an image, global context is often needed to understand what is happening.
For example, a small patch showing a vehicle could be a car on a highway or a boat in a lagoon; without global context, classification is ambiguous.
Shifted windows expands the receptive field by shifting the grid of windows between self-attention layers.
On one layer there is a regular grid of patches; on the next layer, the grid is shifted by half the patch size, but the transformer sees the same input size with different subsets of features.
Doing this after every layer expands the receptive field of the patches.
A patch that originally saw a small part of the image will, after two layers, collect information from a much larger area because each shifted window aggregates features from adjacent patches.
At the edges, shifting the grid causes patches near the image borders to be incomplete squares.
To handle edges, Swin rolls the image into a torus: leftover edge pieces are paired with complementary pieces so that every window remains complete.
This torus handling only affects the edges and ultimately does not matter much, but it is a lot of hassle.
Implementing a 3D SWIN transformer with shifted cubes resulted in convoluted code with many hard-coded shifts and constants.
Both the SWIN transformer and the ViT can serve as good backbones.
A backbone is the largest part of the network that does feature extraction.
By default, the ViT is trained on classification: it extracts features, collects them into a single vector at the end, and does global reasoning about the whole image.
Object detection requires mapping outputs to specific pixels, which is more difficult than global classification.
Object detection involves an image that may contain multiple objects, and for each object you must output the class label and a bounding box.
A bounding box is the rectangle identifying an object's location, usually abbreviated BBox.
Bounding boxes can overlap in any way.
A bounding box is formalized by four numbers: typically x, y for one corner (e.g., bottom-left) and width and height.
A neural network must produce multiple outputs for object detection—one per object.
For each object, the output includes a probability distribution over classes and the four bounding-box numbers.
A neural network cannot have a variable number of outputs; the total number of outputs must be fixed.
If we knew the exact number of objects, the output size would be known, but we do not know the number of objects in advance.
The number of objects in an image can range from a few to hundreds, and it is never known in advance.
To handle variable object counts, we fix a maximal number of objects we expect and provide that many output slots.
When there are fewer objects than the maximum slots, we need a way to mark unused outputs as irrelevant.
The usual fix is to add a confidence output—a probability between zero and one—indicating how sure we are that an object exists in a given slot.
Each output slot consists of a confidence, a class label, and a bounding box.
With two real objects, the desired output is confidence one for those slots and zero for all others.
A loss function is needed to compare the network's fixed-size output to the ground-truth objects.
The ground-truth consists of objects, each with a class and bounding box.

Objects have no natural order, so the network should not be forced to assign specific slots to specific objects; it only matters that real objects appear somewhere with high confidence and other slots have low confidence.
This requires a matching between the ground-truth set and the predicted slots, which is an assignment problem.
By padding the ground truth with “no object” labels up to the fixed number of slots, we can find a bipartite matching that minimizes a cost.
The Hungarian algorithm computes this one-to-one matching, assigning each ground-truth box to the best predictor.
The loss function usually has three components: confidence loss, classification loss, and bounding box loss.
For the confidence loss, confidence should be one for real objects and zero otherwise, typically implemented as log-loss.
Log-loss uses -log(confidence) for present objects and -log(1-confidence) for absent objects.
The classification loss is applied only when an object is present and is the cross-entropy between the predicted class distribution and the ground-truth class.
The bounding box loss is applied only when an object is present and compares the predicted box coordinates to the true rectangle.
Coordinate-based losses treat large and small objects very differently.
For a large object, a moderate coordinate error still yields a lot of overlap and an acceptable prediction.
For a very small object, the same coordinate error can produce zero overlap, making the prediction terrible even though the numerical loss value is similar.
We want the loss to respect perceptual quality and penalize small-object mistakes more.
Some approaches, including the original YOLO, simply accept a coordinate loss.
A more common solution for bounding box loss is to use a loss based on the Intersection over Union (IoU) metric.
IoU between two boxes is the area of their intersection divided by the area of their union.
For the large object, IoU might be 0.6–0.7 (a good match); for the non‑overlapping small object, IoU is exactly zero.
IoU is the default metric for measuring box suitability.
IoU is differentiable when the boxes overlap, giving meaningful gradients because small coordinate changes cause small IoU changes.
When boxes are disjoint, IoU stays zero and the gradient vanishes, providing no learning signal.
Generalized IoU (GIoU) was introduced to provide a useful gradient even without overlap.
The GIoU loss function computes the percentage of the joint bounding box not covered by both predicted and ground-truth boxes.
Moving predictions in the right direction shrinks the joint box and increases the overlap percentage.
Architectures come and go, but loss functions are separate objects that only require gradients to flow through.
Loss functions evolve independently, with dedicated lines of work optimizing losses and architectures separately.
After finding the best assignment between ground-truth and predicted boxes, one must decide which predictions correspond to actual objects.
For a predicted box overlapping a cat, the desired outcome is either to make it the cat box with confidence 1 or treat it as spurious with confidence 0.
In a typical image with few objects, most of the many output boxes should have low confidence.
In practice, this is done with an IoU threshold (e.g., 0.5): predictions above the threshold are counted as ground-truth objects, while those below are ignored.
For clear, easy objects, a detection network often produces multiple bounding boxes around the same object.
At inference time, multiple hypotheses around the same object must be merged into a single box.
The standard merging method is non-maximum suppression (NMS), used only at inference; during training, only the best matching is performed.
The first successful deep learning approach for object detection emerged in 2014 after AlexNet, called R-CNN by Ross Girshick.
R-CNN used an external algorithm, selective search, to generate class-agnostic candidate bounding boxes.
In R-CNN, each proposed box was warped into a square and passed through a CNN pre-trained on ImageNet to predict its class.
The R-CNN classification CNN always assumed the presence of an object and could not explicitly reject background.
The geometric warping in R-CNN to resize proposals was crude.
R-CNN had a third step that took the CNN outputs and passed them through a separate model to classify whether each proposal was a real object.
R-CNN was fragile but the best at the time, running at about a minute per image on a GPU.
All the ideas of two-stage object detection are already present in the original R-CNN architecture.
The core idea of two-stage object detection is to use a backbone network to extract features from a specific part of the input.
In R-CNN, candidate bounding boxes come from an external algorithm, providing a relatively small set of proposals.
Each candidate bounding box is processed through a CNN to extract features and classify its content.
Processing every bounding box completely independently is very slow.
R-CNN required running the CNN forward pass 2,000 times per image, making it impractical.
Fast R-CNN processes the whole image only once.
Fast R-CNN runs the image through a convolutional network but stops earlier than the final classification layer to preserve spatial geometry in the feature tensor.
Candidate bounding boxes are projected onto the feature tensor using a non-trainable region-of-interest (ROI) projection that maps each box to a corresponding spatial region in the feature map.
From each projected ROI, a small detection head containing a classifier and a bounding box regressor is run.
The bounding box regressor can refine the proposal boxes and is trainable because ground truth is available.
Fast R-CNN is orders of magnitude faster than R-CNN because the heavy backbone is run only once and only the tiny detection head is applied per proposal.
A technical challenge in Fast R-CNN is that different proposals have different sizes, while the detection head expects a fixed-size input.
This challenge is solved by ROI pooling.
ROI pooling works by dividing the feature map region into a fixed number of sub-windows and max-pooling within each sub-window.
ROI pooling normalizes the input size and became a standard building block for object detectors.
In Fast R-CNN, the remaining bottleneck was the external algorithm that generated candidate boxes.
Faster R-CNN moves proposal generation inside the network via a region proposal network (RPN).
The RPN operates on the same feature map by sliding a small window and directly predicting plausible bounding boxes.
The RPN outputs a few hundred top proposals, which are then processed by ROI pooling and the detection head for classification and refinement.
Faster R-CNN is a two-stage detector where proposals come from a learned component (the RPN).
Faster R-CNN became the standard object detection approach for many years, until Transformers reshaped the field.
In Faster R-CNN, you can plug in a better backbone without changing the rest of the pipeline to immediately get a better object detector.
Two-stage detection is accurate but relatively slow, and it illustrates key principles of object detection.
Object detection architectures are meta-architectures where a neural network extracts features and performs region proposals, while the detection heads are basically fixed.
The feature extractor can be swapped out, and whenever a better feature extractor appears, object detection improves for free.
One-stage object detection processes the image in a single pass.
In two-stage detection, you first generate proposals, rank them, and apply heavy processing only to the top proposals.
In one-stage detection, you evaluate a set of candidate bounding boxes directly, but you cannot consider every possible rectangle because it would be quadratic in pixels.
Instead, one-stage detectors sample reasonable candidate bounding boxes at a fixed granularity.
The YOLO family best exemplifies one-stage detection with sampling at fixed granularity.
The YOLO family uses a single neural architecture that takes an image, evaluates many candidates in parallel, outputs results, and then ranks them to keep the top predictions.
The original YOLO was followed by YOLOv2, YOLO9000, and YOLOv3.
YOLO9000 handled many classes and introduced hierarchical softmax.
YOLO architectures improve through many small tweaks that each add a few percent to accuracy, collectively yielding a large overall gain.
The central problem of object detection is detecting small objects.
A large object is easily recognized by any architecture.
Detecting small objects exposes a fundamental trade-off.
In a CNN-based detector, you stop at some intermediate feature map.
If you stop too late, the feature grid is coarse, and a small object may lie entirely inside one feature vector, losing its information.
If you stop too early, the grid is fine enough to detect small objects, but then you must search over a huge number of candidate boxes, which is computationally infeasible.
If you restrict fine-scale detection to only small objects, the quadratic complexity disappears.
Multi-stage object detection uses early CNN layers for small objects, later layers for medium objects, and final layers for large objects.
The three scales respectively detect large, medium, and small objects.
Small objects still need global context to be recognized reliably.
One of the most fruitful ideas after Faster R-CNN was the Feature Pyramid Network (FPN).
FPN takes a bottom-up CNN pathway for multi-scale detection and adds top-down connections that fuse features from coarser scales into finer scales.
In FPN, features from the coarsest scale are copied and fused with medium-scale features, which are then fused with fine-scale features.
This injects global context into the fine-scale detector, greatly improving small-object detection.
FPN gave the network the ability to capture global context and became highly influential.
Many subsequent works explored multi-scale, multi-stage object detection.
The EfficientNet family used neural architecture search to find efficient backbones for object detection.
Another family of works searched for optimal post-processing, experimenting with bidirectional feature flow and skip connections.
The appearance of Vision Transformers (ViT) prompted the question whether transformers could simplify object detection.
The lesson of transformers is that often a single excellent architecture can handle a problem if we just let it learn.
Transformers can handle object detection, leading to a family of transformer-based approaches.
The first architecture in this direction is DETR (Detection Transformer).
DETR uses a CNN backbone to extract image features, adds positional encodings, and feeds the resulting sequence of vectors into a transformer encoder.
In DETR, the transformer encoder processes features, and detection happens in the decoder, which is a full encoder-decoder transformer.
The DETR decoder takes a fixed set of object queries (trained vectors or fixed random ones) and passes them through self-attention and cross-attention with encoder outputs.
Each output vector from the DETR decoder is sent to a detection head for classification and bounding box regression.
In DETR, the number of detected objects equals the number of object queries (typically around 100), and most queries learn to output very low confidence.
DETR queries specialize by location rather than class, and because they interact via self-attention, they do not duplicate detections, removing the need for non-maximum suppression.
A major limitation of DETR is its single-scale operation: the CNN backbone produces one feature map, and small objects lost during downsampling cannot be recovered.
Visualizations show that DETR's decoder attention localizes on object boundaries and separates objects cleanly, but the single scale hampers small-object detection.
Deformable DETR addresses the limitations of standard DETR.
Deformable DETR runs on multiple feature scales, like earlier multi-scale methods.
Deformable DETR introduces deformable attention.
In standard DETR, attention concentrates on object boundaries.
Deformable attention avoids the quadratic complexity of global attention.
Deformable attention works by having each attention head look at a small, learned set of positions on the image.
The learned positions are trained jointly with the rest of the network.
Deformable attention allows the transformer to process fine, multi-scale feature maps efficiently without prohibitive cost.
Deformable DETR reduces attention to a small subset of the input tokens.
Subsequent research on DETR variants focused on improving the object queries.
In standard DETR, object queries tend to specialize, with predicted boxes separating over the input image on average.
The specialization learning of object queries happens slowly and is unstable.
The separation of object query predictions does not appear difficult to produce from the start of training.
The next research step used the idea of taking a grid or sampling random points to initialize object queries.
Deformable DETR and Dynamic Anchor Box DETR use anchor boxes as object queries.
In anchor-based DETR variants, object queries are initialized as bounding boxes with coordinates (X, Y, H, W) rather than abstract vectors.
Anchor box initialization allows object queries to be separate from the beginning of training.
Anchor-based object queries provide clear semantics between decoder layers.
Anchor-based object queries enable smarter refinement across decoder layers.
Anchor-based initialization yields better object queries and better anchors in less training time.
Currently, the best object detectors include DINO, its modifications, and Deformable DETR.
DINO, Deformable DETR, and similar architectures share the basic idea of the original DETR.
In the original DETR paradigm, queries representing objects or bounding boxes are inputs to a transformer decoder.
The transformer decoder fills the object queries with content based on the image.
There is a large body of research on DETR variants with many results and architectures.
